summary:
We developed Killa Landing, a web application for planning landings at the lunar south pole. For any landing site and date, it places the Sun and the Earth against each site’s real terrain horizon, built from NASA LRO LOLA topography, with Sun and Earth positions from JPL Horizons. From that it computes solar power and battery state, direct-to-Earth communication windows, landing slope and the risk inside the landing ellipse. It also simulates a physics-based descent and a rover round trip to permanently shadowed ice. A mission planner starts from an ice target and finds the best landing point for every day of a date range.

This matters because the Sun never climbs more than about 1.5° at the south pole. A ridge a few hundred metres high, tens of kilometres away, can leave a site in darkness or cut its link with Earth. The best-lit rims sit beside steep slopes, and the ice hides in permanent shadow, where a rover cannot recharge.

Killa Landing turns those trade-offs into clear numbers and a verdict: Viable, Marginal or Ruled out. Mission planners, educators and the public can compare sites and dates in seconds. Killa means “Moon” in Quechua
details:
What exactly does it do?

Killa Landing answers one question: if a mission lands at this site on this date, will it have sunlight for power, the Earth in view to communicate, and safe ground under it?

  • Compares 22 curated sites: 11 at the south pole on 20 m LOLA terrain (Shackleton rim, Connecting ridge, de Gerlache, Malapert, Mons Mouton, Nobile, Haworth, Cabeus and others) and 11 reference sites (Apollo 11/15/17, Chandrayaan-3, Chang’e-4/6, SLIM, IM-1, IM-3, Blue Ghost, Luna-25). Users can also enter their own coordinates.
    • sunlight and battery state of charge;
    • direct-to-Earth link with a margin over the terrain, optionally requiring a Deep Space Network station;
    • longest night and an estimated temperature;
    • terrain slope and a 3σ landing ellipse;
    • a least-cost rover route to permanently shadowed ice.
  • Simulates a physics-based powered descent (thrust, lunar gravity, propellant and Δv) and a rover round trip: drive to the ice, take samples, and return before the mission ends.
  • Plans missions from the ice. Given an ice target, up to 90 days and a rover workload, it checks 11 hard constraints for every candidate point and day, then returns the best landing point per day, the 5 best days and one-click fixes when nothing passes.
  • Shows everything in 3D (orbit, surface at 2 m, descent, rover) and in 2D (timeline, 360° horizon, alternative dates, seasons 2026–2030, polar map). Users can compare up to 4 scenarios side by side and export CSV and JSON.

How does it work?

  1. Terrain. Offline scripts download LOLA elevation models: 20 m/px around each polar site, 60 m/px for reference sites, 240 m/px out to 300 km. From these they build a 360° horizon mask per site with exact spherical geometry, plus slope maps and yearly illumination maps that mark permanently shadowed regions.
  2. Sky. A JPL Horizons DE441 table gives the Sun and Earth positions in the Moon’s body-fixed frame, every 2 h for 2026–2030. The browser interpolates it. Outside that span, the IAU model from astronomy-engine is used.
  3. Visibility engine. For every minute of the mission, the Sun counts as visible when at least half its disc clears the real horizon. The Earth must clear it by a configurable link margin, 3° by default. Energy, link, night, battery and score all derive from this.
  4. Mission planner. For each day it evaluates candidate points within 1–3 km of the ice target. It runs the rover traverse model (power, battery, slope-derated speed, sampling in shadow) and ranks the days that pass every constraint.
    • JPL Horizons: 1.5″ maximum error over 528 positions;
    • Deep Space Network geometry: 0.0012°;
    • the LROC illumination map: Spearman 0.94–0.98;
    • LROC permanent shadow in Shackleton: IoU 0.98;
    • Moon Trek Earth visibility: Spearman 0.99.
  5. No backend. Everything runs in the browser, with heavy work in a web worker. The processed data, about 65 MB, ships with the app.

What benefits does it have?

  • For mission planners: it screens sites and dates against the planner’s own hardware limits in seconds. It shows why a site fails and what one change would fix it, and the results can be exported for further analysis.
  • For educators and the public: three audience modes (Public, Educator, Planner) and five guided challenges, from finding light to bringing ice back. A “Why?” section and a glossary explain the physics of the poles.
  • Trustworthy: every number traces back to open NASA data and is validated against NASA, JPL and LROC references. One click opens the same point in LROC QuickMap, Moon Trek and a pre-filled JPL Horizons query.
  • Accessible: it runs in any WebGL 2 browser with no installation. The interface is in English, Spanish and Quechua (beta).

What do you hope to achieve?

In the short term, a tool that anyone can use to understand why landing at the lunar south pole is so hard, and that mission teams can use to screen Artemis III and commercial landing sites. Next, we want to plan the whole trip: launch windows, the Earth–Moon trajectory, Δv budgets and relay satellites, all built on the same constraint-based planning approach our team applies to optimise mining operations.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Languages: TypeScript (app and data pipeline), HTML, CSS
  • Frontend and 3D: React 19, three.js, React Three Fiber, drei, Vite, zustand
  • Astronomy: astronomy-engine (IAU lunar rotation model and fallback ephemeris)
  • Data pipeline: Node.js scripts that read LOLA rasters by HTTP range requests and query the JPL Horizons API, Moon Trek WMTS and LROC QuickMap WMS
  • Testing and quality: Vitest, Testing Library, Playwright, ESLint, Prettier, GitHub Actions
  • Hosting: GitHub Pages
  • Hardware: personal laptops; no special hardware
